subject: Copywriting
title: Political Advertising
description: Learn Political Advertising in one minute.

hook.text: The 1964 'Daisy' ad showed a girl picking petals before a nuclear explosion.

buildup.text: The ad never mentioned Barry Goldwater by name. It implied voting for him meant nuclear war.

discovery.text: Political ads use advertising techniques—emotional appeals, simple messages, fear—to sell candidates exactly like.

twist.text: Citizens United (2010) allowed unlimited political ad spending.

climax.text: In 2020, US political campaigns spent $14 billion on advertising.

punchline.text: $14 billion on political ads. Democracy's copy has a price tag.

quiz.question: What did the 1964 'Daisy' ad imply?
options: Voting for Goldwater meant nuclear war

details.summary: Political advertising applies commercial persuasion techniques to elections and governance. From Eisenhower's first TV spots to modern micro-targeted digital ads, campaigns have progressively adopted the tools and psychology of consumer marketing to sell candidates like products.
details.whyItMatters: Political advertising shapes democratic outcomes. Understanding its techniques — emotional appeals, opposition framing, and identity triggers — helps citizens make more informed voting decisions.
takeaways: Eisenhower's 1952 TV spots pioneered political advertising
Negative ads are more memorable than positive ones
Digital micro-targeting allows personalized political persuasion at scale

faq.question: Why do negative political ads work so well?
faq.answer: Negative information carries more cognitive weight than positive information — a phenomenon called negativity bias. Attack ads also create fear and urgency, which motivate action more effectively than hopeful messages. Voters remember what scared them longer than what inspired them.

faq.question: Has digital advertising changed political propaganda?
faq.answer: Dramatically. Digital platforms enable campaigns to deliver different messages to different audiences based on personal data, making propaganda hyper-personalized. A voter in one district sees a completely different version of a candidate than a voter elsewhere.
